result:
At 4:17 in the morning, the refrigerator began to hum in a key I recognized.

Not a melody, exactly. More like the first note of a song someone had once sung from another room, years ago, while washing dishes. The apartment was dark except for the green eye of the microwave clock. It blinked 4:17, 4:17, 4:17, as if time had become stuck on a thought.

Outside, rain had polished the street into a black mirror. Every parked car wore a soft silver outline. The traffic light at the corner changed dutifully from red to green, green to yellow, yellow to red, serving nobody.

I was awake because I had dreamed of a house that didn’t exist.

It stood at the end of a road bordered by tall grass. Its windows glowed gold, and when I looked through them I saw people gathered around a long table. They were all talking at once. I could not hear what they were saying, but I knew they were telling stories about me.

In the dream I approached the front door. Before I could knock, it opened.

A woman I had never seen before smiled at me with the exhausted kindness of someone who had been expecting company for a long time.

“You’re late,” she said.

“For what?” I asked.

She looked past me, toward the dark road.

“For your life.”

Then I woke up.

I went to the kitchen because kitchens are where you go when you need proof that the world still contains ordinary objects. A chipped blue mug. A spoon in the sink. Bread in a plastic bag. A lemon slowly becoming geological on the counter.

I filled the kettle and turned on the stove. The small blue flame appeared beneath it, immediate and obedient. It seemed miraculous, though I had done it thousands of times.

While the water heated, I opened the window.

The city inhaled through wet pavement, gutter leaves, distant diesel, bakery steam. Somewhere a bus sighed at a stop. Somewhere else, a person laughed too loudly, perhaps because they were drunk or lonely or both. A cat walked along a fence with the concentration of a tightrope artist.

There are hours when the world feels less like a place and more like a secret agreement. Everyone has gone home, or is trying to. Everyone has stopped pretending that they understand what they are doing. The buildings stand around us, full of sleeping strangers, each one carrying a private museum of regrets, receipts, passwords, old photographs, unfinished sentences.

The kettle clicked off.

I made tea and sat on the floor by the window, because sometimes a chair makes you feel too confident. The tea was too hot. I held the mug in both hands and watched the rain loosen from the roofs.

Across the street was the laundromat, closed at that hour, its rows of machines visible through the glass. They looked like pale round eyes. I imagined all the clothes turning silently inside them: shirts from interviews, sheets from difficult nights, baby socks, work uniforms, towels that had dried the bodies of people who would never meet.

Everything gets washed eventually, I thought. Or tries to.

A man appeared beneath the awning of the laundromat. He wore a dark coat and carried no umbrella. He stood there for a while, looking at the locked door, though surely he knew it was closed. Then he placed one hand against the glass.

I wondered what he had forgotten inside.

Maybe not clothes. Maybe a name. Maybe an apology he had practiced all week. Maybe the version of himself who had believed there would be more time.

He lowered his hand and walked away.

By five, the rain had thinned to a mist. The sky began changing behind the buildings, not becoming light exactly, but considering the possibility. The first delivery truck rattled down the avenue. A window lit up in the building opposite mine. Behind the curtain, a silhouette moved: someone else awake, someone else performing the small rituals that keep a person attached to a day.

Coffee. Shower. Keys. Shoes.

It struck me then that most lives are not transformed by thunderclaps. They are altered by nearly invisible decisions: answering a message, taking a different street home, saying yes before fear has time to write its speech. A person can become a stranger to themselves in increments so small that no one notices the distance growing.

Or they can return.

I thought again of the woman at the door in my dream.

You’re late, she had said.

Perhaps she had not meant I had missed something. Perhaps she meant that I had arrived at last, carrying all the years I had spent getting there. Perhaps lateness was not failure. Perhaps it was simply the shape of a long journey.

The microwave clock changed to 5:03.

The refrigerator hummed its low, familiar note.

I drank the last of my tea, now lukewarm and bitter, and decided that when morning came properly, I would buy flowers. Nothing grand. Just the cheap kind wrapped in paper outside the grocery store: daisies, maybe, or tulips with their heads bowed as if thinking hard.

I would put them in a jar on the table.

I would call someone I missed.

I would walk without headphones and let the city make its own music.

Outside, the traffic light changed to green.

This time, a car passed through it.
